passage:
"Okay, dinner quiz!" said Dilnaz. "Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?"
"Iron!" Saif shouted before she'd finished. He was eight and banged the table. "Iron, obviously. Iron is super heavy."
"Are you sure?" Ammi asked.
"A hundred percent. I know this. Cotton is fluffy."
Zeenat Khala smiled into her dal. "Want to bet your last laddoo?"
"Yes! Easy laddoo."
Dilnaz waited. "A kilo is a kilo. They weigh the same."
Saif's mouth opened. Nothing came out. "No… but iron is…"
"Heavy for its size," said Khala. "A kilo of cotton is just a big pile."
Saif stared. "I was so sure."
Khala slid the laddoo back to him. "Being sure isn't the same as knowing, beta. Next time, think first, then bet."

qa.q: What did Saif bet on his answer?
qa.a: His last laddoo.

qa.q: Why did Saif feel a hundred percent sure the iron was heavier?
qa.a: Iron feels heavy and cotton looks fluffy, so the answer seemed obvious to him. The feeling of being right came faster than thinking about what a kilo means.

qa.q: What could Saif try the next time he feels completely sure of an answer?
qa.a: He could pause and explain his reason out loud before shouting or betting, which might show him the gap in his thinking.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel watching Saif so confident about the wrong answer?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably finds it a bit funny and waits kindly instead of mocking him, maybe remembering being fooled by the same riddle.

grounding: A young boy is completely sure of a riddle's answer, bets on it, and is stunned to learn he was wrong.

passage: I'm Uday, and at ten I was a skinny boy who thought he could beat anyone. That summer, at the club pool, my cousin Pallavi said, "Race you, two lengths." I'd watched swimmers on TV all week. I knew exactly how they did it: arms like windmills, kick hard, don't breathe much. "Easy," I said. "I'll wait for you at the end." I had only ever paddled in the shallow end. The whistle blew. I windmilled. I swallowed half the pool. By the middle I was holding the rope, coughing, while Pallavi touched the wall and turned around. I couldn't believe it. In my head I'd already won. A lifeguard helped me out. Pallavi didn't laugh. She said, "Want me to teach you breathing?" I said yes, very quietly.

qa.q: How many lengths did Pallavi say they should race?
qa.a: Two lengths.

qa.q: Why was Uday so sure he would win?
qa.a: He felt confident after watching swimmers on TV all week, sure he knew exactly how to do it. Knowing what it looked like felt the same as being able to do it.

qa.q: What choice did Uday make after the race that helped him learn?
qa.a: He said yes when Pallavi offered to teach him breathing, instead of pretending he had lost by bad luck.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt seeing Uday holding the rope and coughing?
qa.a: She was probably worried for a moment and then kind, since she didn't laugh and offered to teach him.

grounding: A boy is sure he can beat his cousin in a swimming race after watching it on TV, and is stunned when he can't finish.

passage: On his uncle's farm outside Sangli, Ganesh, sixteen, had driven the tractor twice, both times with his aunt Vasudha beside him on the flat stretch near the shed. On the third morning he told his cousin Pooja, "I've got it. I'll take it to the far field myself." "Alone? Aai said—" "It's simple. Clutch, gear, go. I've done it twice." Vasudha came out of the kitchen wiping her hands. "Ganesh, tell me how you'd go down the slope by the canal." He shrugged. "Same as on the flat." Vasudha shook her head. "That's the part you haven't done. On a slope you need a low gear before you start down." Ganesh went red. He hadn't known that at all. Two tries on flat ground had felt like knowing everything. "Okay," he said. "Will you sit with me on the slope?" Pooja grinned. "I'm coming too."

qa.q: How many times had Ganesh driven the tractor?
qa.a: He had driven the tractor twice.

qa.q: Why did Ganesh think driving to the far field alone would be simple?
qa.a: Two easy tries on flat ground felt like he had mastered it. He didn't know enough yet to realise the slope was a different skill.

qa.q: Which question from Vasudha was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: Asking how he would go down the slope by the canal. His answer showed him, not her, the gap in what he knew, so he asked her to sit with him.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when Ganesh announced he'd go alone?
qa.a: Pooja seemed uneasy, starting to remind him what Aai said, and then relieved and cheerful once he agreed to have Vasudha along.

grounding: A teenage boy thinks he can drive a tractor alone after two tries, until his aunt asks him about a part he has never done.

passage: The hostel allotment list went up at six on a stormy evening, and Usha's name wasn't on it. She read it twice, rain dripping off the notice board's plastic cover. She had been so sure. "I'm in the top twenty of the batch, they always take the top twenty," she'd told everyone. So she had given notice on her rented room, which ended tomorrow. She hadn't looked at any other rooms. When Imran had asked, "What if the list is different this year?" she had laughed. Now her two bags were packed, the auto drivers weren't coming out in this rain, and she had nowhere to sleep tomorrow night. Imran found her under the canteen awning, staring at nothing. "I didn't even let myself think it could go wrong," she said. "That's why it feels like the floor fell." He handed her his umbrella. "Let's call your old landlord first."

qa.q: What time did the hostel allotment list go up?
qa.a: At six on a stormy evening.

qa.q: Why does Usha say it feels like "the floor fell"?
qa.a: She had been completely certain and never allowed any doubt, so she made no backup plan. The shock is bigger because she had no room in her mind for this outcome.

qa.q: What choice earlier could have left Usha some margin, and what should she do first now?
qa.a: Earlier, she could have kept looking at other rooms or waited to give notice until the list came out. Now, calling the old landlord first, as Imran suggests, is a sensible step.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when he finds Usha under the canteen awning?
qa.a: He is probably sorry for her and a little worried, and chooses practical help over saying "I told you so."

grounding: A student so sure of a hostel seat gives up her room with no backup, and the rejection hurts more because she never allowed doubt.

passage: Kavitha had already bought the frame for the certificate. The college's startup grant would be announced on Friday, and she was certain her project, a repair-and-resell shop for old school uniforms in Chennai, would win. She'd told her parents at dinner. She'd borrowed three thousand from her cousin to print banners with "Winner" left blank to fill in later. When her friend Ayesha said, "Maybe keep a plan B, just in case?" Kavitha said, "Why plan to lose?" On Friday, in the packed seminar hall, the names were read out. Hers wasn't one of them. She sat through the claps with a fixed smile. Outside by the bike stand she finally cried. "It's not just losing," she told Ayesha. "I made everyone believe it too. And I have no idea what to do on Monday." Ayesha put an arm around her shoulders and waited.

qa.q: What had Kavitha already bought before the announcement?
qa.a: The frame for the certificate.

qa.q: Why is losing so painful for Kavitha?
qa.a: She had been so sure that she told her parents, borrowed money and printed banners, leaving no space for doubt. Now she faces the loss plus the embarrassment of having no plan.

qa.q: When Ayesha suggested a plan B, what choice could Kavitha have made instead?
qa.a: She could have said, "Good idea," and quickly listed what she would do if she didn't win, such as other grants or starting smaller, without giving up hope.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel standing with Kavitha by the bike stand?
qa.a: Ayesha probably feels sad for Kavitha and chooses to comfort her quietly instead of reminding her of the plan B conversation.

grounding: A student certain she will win a startup grant makes no backup plan and is hurt more deeply when she loses.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Rao Caterers kitchen, Tuesday. Written by Aparna.
Akash, our newest cook, told the team this morning that he would have all 600 sweet boxes for the Kulkarni wedding ready by Thursday noon. "No problem at all, I've done big orders." He said it with such certainty that two of the helpers started planning their Thursday off. I've seen this before, so I didn't argue and I didn't just nod. I asked him, "What's your best case, your likely case and your worst case?" He paused. Best: Wednesday night. Likely: Thursday morning. Worst: if the khoa delivery is late, Friday. Friday is too late for the wedding. So we ordered the khoa a day earlier and kept one helper on standby for Thursday. Akash looked a bit deflated at first, but later he told me, "I never think about the worst case. That was useful."

qa.q: How many sweet boxes did Akash promise for the Kulkarni wedding?
qa.a: All 600 sweet boxes, ready by Thursday noon.

qa.q: How did Akash feel after being asked for a worst case, and why?
qa.a: He looked a bit deflated at first because his confident promise was being questioned. Later he found it useful, since he had never thought about what could go wrong.

qa.q: What did Aparna do instead of arguing or blindly trusting Akash?
qa.a: Aparna asked for a best, likely and worst case. When the worst case showed a problem, the khoa was ordered earlier and kept a helper on standby.

qa.q: How might the helpers who had planned Thursday off see Akash's promise now?
qa.a: They may be a bit disappointed to lose the day off but relieved the team won't be caught short if the khoa is late.

grounding: A catering supervisor sees a new cook promise fast delivery with total confidence and asks for best, likely and worst cases instead of arguing.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today at the NGO meeting, Gopika said she'd translate the whole 80-page health-worker manual into Marathi by Monday. "Easy, I'm fast," she said, and everyone relaxed. I'm the team lead, and part of me wanted to believe her, because the funders are waiting. Another part of me remembered how long the last 20 pages took. I didn't want to embarrass her in front of everyone, and I didn't want to just say okay either. After the meeting I asked her over chai, "What's the fastest you could do it, what's realistic, and what could go wrong?" She laughed first, then thought. Fastest Monday. Realistic Thursday. Worst, if the medical terms need checking, two weeks. Two weeks! So I've told the funders "next Friday" and asked Rohini to check terms in parallel. Gopika seemed relieved, actually.
Sangeeta

qa.q: How many pages is the health-worker manual?
qa.a: It is an 80-page manual.

qa.q: Why did part of Sangeeta want to believe Gopika?
qa.a: The funders were waiting, so a quick, confident promise felt like a relief. Believing it would have made Sangeeta's own worry go away.

qa.q: What choice did Sangeeta make over chai, and how did it help?
qa.a: Sangeeta privately asked for the fastest, realistic and worst case. That revealed a possible two-week delay, so Sangeeta set a safer date and got Rohini to help.

qa.q: Why might Gopika have seemed relieved after the conversation?
qa.a: Gopika may have felt pressure from her own bold promise, and a realistic plan with help took that weight off.

grounding: A team lead's diary shows the lead asking a confident colleague for a range and worst case instead of trusting or scolding the promise.

passage: Every Monday morning at her desk in a Hyderabad architecture office, Ayesha opened a small spreadsheet and typed three predictions. "Client approves the facade by Friday: 80%." "Structural drawings back this week: 60%." "The site visit happens on time: 90%." On the last Friday of each month she went back and marked what really happened. Her colleague Kavitha found it odd at first. "You're just guessing." "I'm checking my guesses," Ayesha said. After three months a pattern was clear. When she said 90% about her own work, she was right almost every time. But when she said 80% about clients approving things fast, she was right only about half the time. "So my sure feeling about clients is too sure," she told Kavitha. Next week, she typed, "Client approves by Friday: 55%." Then she warned the team to keep a buffer.

qa.q: On which day did Ayesha go back and mark what really happened?
qa.a: On the last Friday of each month.

qa.q: How does Ayesha seem to feel when she discovers her client predictions were too sure?
qa.a: She seems curious rather than upset, treating the result as useful information about where her confidence can and cannot be trusted.

qa.q: What change did Ayesha make after seeing the pattern, and why does it help?
qa.a: She lowered her client prediction to 55% and told the team to keep a buffer, so plans match how things usually go.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's view of the spreadsheet change over the three months?
qa.a: Kavitha first thought it was just guessing, but seeing Ayesha adjust real plans could make Kavitha see it as a smart habit.

grounding: A young architect writes predictions with percentages, checks them monthly, and learns where her confident feelings are reliable.

passage:
"Bhavna, it's Sunday. Why are you marking a notebook at breakfast?"
"It's my prediction book, Kunal. Every January I write down guesses with percentages."
Her brother leaned over. "'Get the Pune account: 90%.' Did you?"
"Yes. Tick."
"'Team wins the quarterly award: 85%.'"
"No." She drew a cross. "And look. 'Boss approves leave in first try: 80%.' Cross again."
Mummy poured the tea. "So your feeling is wrong?"
"Not always. When it's about my own clients, I'm usually right. When it depends on other people's decisions, I'm too sure."
Kunal laughed. "So you're overconfident about everyone else."
"About guessing what they'll do, yes. Next year I'll put those lower."
"Can I start one?" Kunal asked.
"Only if you check it in December."

qa.q: What was Bhavna's prediction about the Pune account?
qa.a: Get the Pune account: 90%.

qa.q: How does Bhavna feel about the crosses in her book?
qa.a: She seems calm and interested rather than embarrassed, because the crosses show her exactly where her confidence is too high.

qa.q: What does Bhavna decide to do differently next year, and why?
qa.a: She will give lower percentages to predictions that depend on other people's decisions, because her checks show she is too sure about those.

qa.q: Why might Kunal want to start his own prediction book?
qa.a: Seeing his sister learn something useful about herself from ticks and crosses makes the habit look practical and a bit fun.

grounding: At a family breakfast, a young woman checks her yearly percentage predictions and finds where her confidence is and isn't reliable.

passage: I'm Siddharth, and I sit behind Manoj in Class 10. I'll tell you what happened, though I don't really know what goes on in his head. Over the holidays he watched a few videos about the Indus Valley script. Four or five, I think. He came back saying one video had "basically cracked it." In history class, when Pillai sir said nobody has deciphered the script yet, Manoj put up his hand. "Sir, that's outdated. It's been solved. I watched it." Sir asked, "By whom? Which symbols? How was it checked?" Manoj said, "The video explained it all," and looked annoyed. Sir didn't laugh. He said, "Bring the source, and let's look at it together on Friday." On Friday Manoj brought the video. It was one person's theory, and the comments were full of experts disagreeing. Manoj went quiet for the whole period.

qa.q: Why might Manoj feel sure he knew more than Pillai sir?

qa.q: What did Pillai sir choose to do instead of laughing, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked Manoj to bring the source and look at it together on Friday. Seeing the disagreement himself taught Manoj more than being mocked would.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel watching Manoj go quiet on Friday?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel a bit sorry for Manoj, and maybe a little relieved that sir handled it without embarrassing him in front of everyone.

passage:
Monday. Darshan, fifteen, had watched French videos all weekend: greetings, café phrases, a funny one about verbs. In class he corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant" and said, "Honestly, the videos teach it better." A few classmates giggled. Urmila ma'am just said, "Wonderful. Then you can help me on Thursday."
Thursday. She gave him a short paragraph to read aloud and translate: a letter from a French student about her village. Darshan got through "Bonjour" and stopped. Past tense verbs. Words he'd never seen. He tried twice and his ears went hot. "I didn't know it had all this," he mumbled.
The next Monday. He stayed after class. "Ma'am, I think the videos gave me the easy parts. I didn't even know what I didn't know." Urmila ma'am smiled. "That's the first real step. Want the grammar sheet?" He took two.

qa.q: Which word's pronunciation did Darshan correct?
qa.a: He corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant."

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel he knew French better than his teacher on Monday?
qa.a: A weekend of videos gave him easy phrases that felt like a lot. He didn't know enough yet to see how much grammar and vocabulary he was missing.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Darshan choose to do after it?
qa.a: Trying to read the paragraph on Thursday showed him the gaps. The next Monday he stayed after class, admitted it and took two grammar sheets.

qa.q: How might Urmila ma'am have felt when Darshan corrected her in front of the class?
qa.a: She may have felt a flicker of annoyance, but she stayed calm and found a way to let him discover the gaps himself.

grounding: A teenage boy thinks a weekend of videos makes him better at French than his teacher, until a reading task shows him what he's missing.

passage: The robotics lab at the engineering college smelled of solder at nine in the evening. Aadhya, a second-year, had spent a week on control theory videos and notes, and it all clicked. "I get PID now," she told Yash, the senior who ran the club. "I can tune any robot." The first test on the flat floor went perfectly. Then Yash put the line-following robot on the new track with ramps and sharp curves. It wobbled, overshot and crashed into the wall. Aadhya changed the numbers. Worse. She changed them again. By eleven she was sitting on a stool, arms crossed. "I thought I understood it. Now I feel like I know nothing." Yash sat on the bench opposite, rubbing his eyes. "That's where I was in second year too. The first week you know the idea. Now you're learning the real thing." She looked at the robot, then pulled her notebook closer.

qa.q: What happened when Yash put the robot on the new track?
qa.a: It wobbled, overshot and crashed into the wall.

qa.q: Why does Aadhya suddenly feel like she knows nothing?
qa.a: After feeling like an expert, the harder track left her frustrated and discouraged, and the drop in confidence feels like failure even though it is part of learning.

qa.q: What choice does Aadhya make at the end, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She pulls her notebook closer and keeps working. Staying with the problem through the dip is how real skill grows.

qa.q: How might Yash see Aadhya's frustration?
qa.a: Yash recognises it from his own second year and sees it as a normal stage, so he encourages her rather than worrying.

grounding: A student who just learned a control method feels expert until a harder track humbles her, and a senior tells her the dip is normal.

passage:
Dear Sachin sir,
You taught us the inverted pyramid in first year: most important facts first, then details. After that class I honestly felt like a journalist. I wrote three stories for the college paper in a week, all neat, all praised.
Then this month the city newspaper gave us interns the municipal budget to cover. Pages of numbers, departments I'd never heard of, two councillors saying opposite things. I didn't even know which fact was "most important." I rewrote my first paragraph eleven times. For the first time I felt like a fake.
My editor said that's normal, and that the people who feel fine at this stage usually haven't understood the story yet. That helped a little.
Could I show you my draft next week? I think I need to learn the harder parts properly now.
With respect,
Kashish

qa.q: How many times did Kashish rewrite the first paragraph?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Kashish feel "like a fake" this month?
qa.a: After quick success with simple stories, the budget story left Kashish unsure and overwhelmed by how much was still unknown. The confidence dropped before the deeper skill had time to grow.

qa.q: What choice does Kashish make at the end of the letter, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Asking Sachin sir to look at the draft next week. Seeking help during the dip turns it into learning instead of giving up.

qa.q: How might Sachin sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might feel proud that Kashish is facing the harder parts honestly and glad to be asked for help.

grounding: A journalism student felt expert after learning one method, then struggled with a hard story and sees the dip as a sign to keep learning.

passage: The pumping station on the edge of Nashik lost power at two in the morning during the worst storm of the year. The backup pump wouldn't start, and water was rising in the basement. Rajni, twenty-four and the junior engineer on duty, traced the fault in twenty minutes by torchlight: a burnt relay and a wrongly set timer. She swapped the relay from a spare panel and reset the timer. The pump roared. When the supervisor, Vishal, arrived soaked at three, it was already done. "How did you find it so fast?" Rajni shrugged. "Anyone would have. It was just the relay." "Anyone? The last two engineers took a whole day with that panel." She shook her head. "They must have been busy." Later he asked her to lead the new training sessions. She said, "Maybe someone more senior?" Vishal frowned. "No. You."

qa.q: What was the fault Rajni found?
qa.a: A burnt relay and a wrongly set timer.

qa.q: Why does Rajni say "Anyone would have"?
qa.a: Rajni seems uncomfortable with praise, and because the fix felt easy to her, she assumes it would be easy for everyone. Her skill makes her notice how simple the problem was, not how rare her ability is.

qa.q: What choice could Rajni make when Vishal offers her the training sessions?
qa.a: She could accept and treat his evidence, the last two engineers taking a whole day, as a fair measure of her ability instead of her own doubts.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Rajni's work that night?
qa.a: He sees it as exceptional, since others struggled with the same panel for a day, and is frustrated that she doesn't see it herself.

grounding: A skilled young engineer fixes a pump fault fast during a storm but assumes anyone could have, and doubts she should lead training.

passage: The internal job post for senior design engineer at the Pune car-parts factory closed on Friday, and Indu hadn't applied. Her colleague Vaibhav found her at the canteen with a plate of misal. "You're the one who fixed the brake-bracket design in two days. The whole team was stuck for a month." "It was just a geometry thing," Indu said. "If you know the tool, it's obvious." "It wasn't obvious to me. Or to the senior people." She pushed the misal around. "Every time I learn something, I see ten more things I don't know. The guys who applied seem so sure." "Maybe that's because they see less," Vaibhav said. "You notice the gaps because you know the field." Indu was quiet. "You really think I should apply?" "I think you're the only one who's asking that question." She opened the job post on her phone before lunch ended.

qa.q: How long had the whole team been stuck on the brake-bracket design?
qa.a: The whole team was stuck for a month.

qa.q: Why does Indu feel less sure than the colleagues who applied?
qa.a: Indu feels insecure because each thing she learns shows her more she doesn't know. The easy fix felt obvious to her, so she didn't count it as special.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation with Vaibhav?
qa.a: When Vaibhav said Indu notices the gaps because she knows the field. That helped Indu see the doubt differently and open the job post.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel about Indu not applying?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems frustrated and wants Indu to be recognised, having seen her solve what the whole team couldn't.

grounding: A skilled young engineer thinks her fix was obvious and doubts herself, while less aware colleagues apply confidently.

passage: In the staff room of the government girls' school, Sharmila, the senior English teacher, read the lesson plan her new colleague Minakshi had written. "It's perfect," Minakshi said. "They'll finish the whole poem, write an essay and do a quiz in one period." Sharmila remembered a head teacher years ago who had laughed at her first plan in front of everyone. She had defended it for a month out of pride. So she didn't laugh. "It looks lively. Can you walk me through it minute by minute? Forty minutes, starting from the bell." Minakshi began. "Five minutes reading. Then…" She counted on her fingers. By the essay, she had used fifty-five minutes. She stopped. "Oh." "Last year my class took fifteen minutes just on the first stanza," Sharmila said. "Here's what I noticed then." Minakshi pulled out a pencil and started cutting.

qa.q: How many minutes had Minakshi used by the time she reached the essay?
qa.a: By the essay, she had used fifty-five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi think her plan was perfect?
qa.a: Minakshi felt confident because on paper the plan looked complete, and without having taught this poem she couldn't yet see how long each part would really take.

qa.q: What did Sharmila choose to do instead of laughing, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked Minakshi to walk through the plan minute by minute. Counting it out made the gap clear to Minakshi herself, so she started cutting without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel watching Minakshi discover the timing problem?
qa.a: Sharmila likely feels patient and sympathetic, remembering being laughed at over her own first plan, so she lets Minakshi find the problem instead of mocking her.

grounding: A senior teacher asks a confident new colleague to walk through a lesson plan minute by minute, so the gaps show without ridicule.

passage:
Subject: Your first chapter edit, a few specific things
Hi Tejas,
Thank you for turning in the edit of Chapter 3 so quickly. You mentioned you felt it was "fully clean," and I can see how hard you worked on the commas.
Before we send it to the author, I'd like you to try something. Could you write out, step by step, how you checked the dates and names? Not what you changed, but how you checked.
I'm asking because I found a few things. On page 12, the author calls the grandmother "Rukmini," and on page 19 "Rukmani." On page 27, the war ends in 1971 and the child is born "two years later, in 1972."
These are easy to miss. I missed plenty in my first year. Walking through the process usually shows where the gaps are.
Let's talk tomorrow at 11.
Vinita

qa.q: What year was the child born according to page 27?
qa.a: In 1972, "two years later" after the war ended in 1971.

qa.q: Why might Tejas have felt the chapter was "fully clean"?
qa.a: Tejas had worked hard on the commas and fixed what was visible. As a newcomer, Tejas didn't yet know to check names and dates across pages, so those gaps stayed hidden.

qa.q: What did Vinita ask Tejas to do, and why is it better than just listing the mistakes?
qa.a: Vinita asked Tejas to write out step by step how the dates and names were checked. Walking through the process lets Tejas find the gap first-hand, which sticks better than being corrected.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel about sending Tejas this email?
qa.a: Vinita probably feels supportive but careful, wanting Tejas to learn the checking process without feeling judged, which is why Vinita praises the commas and admits missing plenty in the first year.

grounding: A mentor emails a new copy editor specific examples and asks for the checking process step by step so the gaps show without being pointed out bluntly.

passage: The Osaka school relay ended with the red team crossing first. Hiroshi, nine, had spent the race gripping the rope, shouting for white, his team. "Come on, come on!" Afterwards, eating onigiri on the grass with his sister Noa, he said, "I knew we'd lose. Our third runner is slow. It was obvious." Noa raised an eyebrow. "This morning you said white would win by miles. You bet me your dessert." "No, I didn't. I said it might be close." "You said 'by miles.' Twice." Hiroshi looked at his onigiri. "Well… I sort of knew." Noa laughed. "You knew after it happened." Hiroshi frowned, trying to remember what he really thought that morning. Now the loss seemed certain too. He handed her the dessert anyway.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi bet Noa?
qa.a: His dessert.

qa.q: Why does Hiroshi now feel he knew his team would lose?
qa.a: After the race, the slow third runner seems like an obvious reason, so his mind rewrites the morning's hope into a prediction of losing. Now the loss feels like it was always certain.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi do before the next race to see what he really expected?
qa.a: He could write down his prediction before the race, so afterwards he can check what he actually thought instead of relying on memory.

qa.q: How might Noa see Hiroshi's claim that he knew all along?
qa.a: She finds it funny, since she clearly remembers him saying "by miles" twice, and gently points out that he only knew after it happened.

grounding: A boy says he knew his team would lose the relay, though that morning he had bet they would win easily.

passage: In the boys' hostel common room, twenty children crowded round the TV for the badminton final. Chaitanya, eleven, was loudly sure: "Green shirt will win. He's the champion. No chance for the other one." In the third game, the younger player in blue won every long rally. When blue won the final point, the room exploded. Chaitanya folded his arms. "I knew it. Green was getting tired from the first game. Anyone could see." Lalit sir, the warden, stacked chairs. "Chaitanya, what did you say at the start?" "I said… green might be tired." "I heard 'no chance for the other one.'" A few boys laughed. Chaitanya went pink. "It felt like I knew," he said quietly. Lalit sir nodded. "It always does, afterwards."

qa.q: Who won the final point?
qa.a: The younger player in blue.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya feel he knew green would lose?
qa.a: Once the match ended, the signs of green getting tired seemed obvious, so his memory changed his confident prediction into "I knew it." It genuinely feels true to him.

qa.q: How could Chaitanya check his memory next time he feels he "knew it all along"?
qa.a: He could say his prediction out loud or write it down before the match, then compare it honestly with the result.

qa.q: How might Lalit sir feel when Chaitanya says "It felt like I knew"?
qa.a: He probably feels kind towards him, glad Chaitanya noticed the trick his memory played, and his reply shows it happens to everyone.

grounding: A boy watching a badminton final claims he knew the champion would lose, though he had said the opposite at the start.
